In the correctly time-matched 10-month window, spending actually rose $308B -- not $147B -- comfortably exceeding, not being exceeded by, the $242B combined factor, which directly contradicts the article's inference that underlying spending 'might even have shrunk.' Second, a category error: the tariff refund is a revenue-side reduction (netted against customs receipts per Treasury's own accounting, confirmed in this table's receipts-range line code), not government spending; adding it to a spending item (interest) and calling the sum an increase in 'spending' misclassifies it. Third, the $147B figure itself is artificially depressed by a one-time payment-calendar shift (Aug 1, 2026 falling on a Saturday) that Treasury itself flagged and adjusted for in the same week's reporting -- a confound the article does not mention. Every individual dollar figure the article cites is independently accurate; the inference built by combining them is not.
